newsitem.title: UK: Dutch C. Banker Duisenberg wants strict EMU rules.
newsitem.headline: Dutch C. Banker Duisenberg wants strict EMU rules.

text.p: Wim Duisenberg, the Dutchman who is tipped to head the European Central Bank if European Monetary Union goes ahead, believes that rules for entry into EMU should be applied "very strictly."

"That is the only way in which you can build a new currency which can have confidence in the market as being a stable and hard currency," Duisenberg, currently governor of the Dutch central bank, told the Daily Telegraph in an interview.
The Maastricht criteria call for countries who want to join EMU to achieve price stability and keep government debt under strict control.

Noting that he was 99 percent certain EMU would start on time in 1999, Duisenberg told the Telegraph that "at least eight and possibly eleven countries" could be ready to join on the proposed start date of January 1999.

Commenting on individual countries, he said the imposition of strict rules would not preclude countries like Italy joining, but said Italy was unlikely to make it in the first wave, but would certainly be in before the year 2002.
"To my mind, very soon afterwards means well before the full introduction of euros notes and coins. So yes, within two years of the start," Duisenberg said.

He termed Britain's potential rejection of EMU "a big mistake," saying that interest rates in Britain could halve to German or Dutch levels if it joined and that the benefits of a single trading bloc would be huge.

The British government is adopting a wait-and-see approach to EMU, but the decision must be taken soon, Duisenberg told the newspaper, although he refused to comment on whether Britain could be amongst the first wave in 1999.

The newspaper said: "(The British government) could not leave the decision to until the end of next year, just a few months before "the moment of truth' in early 1998, when decisions will be made on which countries can enter will be made."
